title: The Mary Celeste, 1872: A Ship With No One Aboard. Where Did the Ten Go?
description:
On the afternoon of December 4, 1872, a ship was still sailing on the Atlantic between the Azores and Portugal: sails set, not one barrel of cargo missing, enough food and water for half a year, and not one of the ten people on board anywhere to be found.

This episode goes through the file from start to finish: the deck the mate saw when he climbed aboard, how the Attorney General in Gibraltar came to treat it as a murder case, the December 23 survey list of what was missing and what remained, what the lab concluded about the marks on the sword that looked "like blood", how an 1884 story put "the boats were all still there" into popular memory, where that hot meal came from, and, after the theories are stopped by the evidence one by one, the number that only turned up when the cargo was unloaded in Genoa.

Every popular version is labeled as a later addition; where there is no settled answer, the episode says so. The source of every number, date and quotation is listed in the references below.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone; living or recent people are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-10

chapters.decide-sail: The mate takes her to Gibraltar
chapters.surveyor-list: Navigation tools gone, six months' food left

mc1a.text: December 4, 1872, in the afternoon, on the Atlantic.

mc1b.text: The captain of a British sailing ship raises his telescope.

mc1c.text: The ship in the distance has crooked sails and moves unsteadily.

mc1d.text: She is the Mary Celeste, with ten people on board.

mc1e.text: The first mate, Deveau, rows across in a small boat and climbs on deck.

mc1f.text: There is no one on deck, and no one at the wheel.

mc1g.text: The fore hatch is open, and over a meter of water has collected in the hold.

mc1h.text: Yet the ship is still sailing, and not one barrel of cargo is missing.

mc1i.text: A sounding rod, for measuring water depth, lies on the deck.

mc1k.text: A thick rope trails from the stern, one end broken, hanging in the sea.

mc1l.text: Why would ten people leave a ship that could still sail?

mc2a.text: Deveau didn't wait for help; he decided to sail the ship away himself.

mc2b.text: His ship was the Dei Gratia, and her captain was Morehouse.

mc2c.text: He kept two sailors with him, and the three of them took the empty ship east.

mc2d.text: The British ship reached Gibraltar first; the Mary Celeste docked the next morning.

mc2e.text: Salvage money isn't finders keepers; a court has to award it.

mc2f.text: Five days later the court sat, and Attorney General Solly-Flood was there.

mc2g.text: He looked at Deveau and felt the story didn't add up.

mc2h.text: His theory was that the crew had secretly drunk that alcohol,

mc2i.text: killed the captain while drunk, and escaped aboard another ship.

mc2j.text: The captain he meant was Briggs, 37, from Massachusetts.

mc2k.text: He'd been at sea for more than ten years and had bought a share in this ship.

mc2l.text: Remember this one thing; it will come back.

mc2m.text: On November 7 he left New York with wife Sarah and two-year-old daughter Sophia.

mc2n.text: The other seven were crew he had hired, and they were bound for Genoa.

mc2o.text: The problem is, those 1,701 barrels held industrial alcohol.

mc2p.text: It wasn't for drinking, and only one barrel had been opened.

mc2q.text: And the captain himself never touched a drop.

mc2r.text: But that isn't the strangest part.

mc3a.text: On December 23, a surveyor sent by the court boarded the ship.

mc3b.text: Even a diver went down to look at her bottom.

mc3c.text: The hull was entirely undamaged, and the masts were sound.

mc3d.text: The surveyor also noted that she hadn't met especially bad weather.

mc3e.text: On a shelf in the mate's cabin, a bottle of sewing-machine oil still stood upright.

mc3f.text: Oddly, on the day the mate boarded, the galley stove had been knocked out of place.

mc3g.text: That day the binnacle was askew too, and the glass over the compass was broken.

mc3h.text: The surveyor also saw marks on both sides of the bow, like knife cuts.

mc3i.text: The sextant and the chronometer were not on board.

mc3j.text: Those are what you use to find your position at sea.

mc3k.text: The navigation book and the ship's register had been taken too.

mc3l.text: In fact, more had stayed behind: the logbook still lay open on the table.

mc3m.text: Clothes hung in their places, and the child's clothes and toys were there too.

mc3n.text: Six months of food and water, and none of it taken.

mc3o.text: On one side, the rail had been lowered, as if to launch a boat the usual way.

mc3p.text: My view: stove and binnacle aside, this looks like a hurried but orderly exit.

mc3q.text: What they took were the tools for finding the way; they left the food and clothes.

mc3r.text: A slate on the table too: its last entry was made on the morning of November 25.

mc3s.text: The position: about 11 kilometers off Santa Maria Island in the Azores.

mc3t.text: From that entry to Deveau climbing on deck, nine days are blank.

mc3u.text: What happened on board during that gap?

mc3v.text: Even the date she was found conflicts: some records say the 4th, the log the 5th.

mc3w.text: There was also the captain's sword, in its sheath, under the bed.

mc3x.text: The blade had a film of marks on it, as if blood had been smeared and wiped off.

mc3y.text: They sent the sword to be tested.

mc4a.text: The test's conclusion took just two words: not blood.

mc4b.text: It was signed by a doctor and dated January 30, 1873.

mc4c.text: Then what about those knife-like marks on the bow?

mc4d.text: Over a month later, the captain of a US warship said it was wood torn by the sea.

mc4e.text: The murder theory fell away, piece by piece.

mc4f.text: Deveau was called back from Genoa to testify in court a third time.

mc4g.text: But the news had already reached the other side of the Atlantic.

mc4h.text: An American newspaper's headline: the ship's officers, believed murdered at sea.

mc4i.text: That March, the court awarded salvage money: 1,700 pounds.

mc4j.text: That was only about a fifth of the ship and cargo's estimated value.

mc4k.text: The court even had a word of blame for Captain Morehouse.

mc4l.text: My view: an award that small means the court itself didn't quite believe it either.

mc4m.text: But what the whole world came to remember was a hot meal still on the table.

mc5a.text: Twelve years later, in 1884, a British magazine ran a short story.

mc5b.text: The author didn't sign it; he later went on to write Sherlock Holmes.

mc5c.text: The story even got the ship's name wrong, spelling it another way.

mc5d.text: He wrote that the boats were still on their davits, and the ship was towed into port.

mc5e.text: Neither of those is in the court record.

mc5f.text: Readers took it for a true account.

mc5g.text: That hot meal isn't even in this story.

mc5h.text: It was added by others, as they retold it.

mc5i.text: What the record at the time says is: no food or drink of any kind on the table.

mc5j.text: The tea still warm in the cups crept in the same way.

mc5k.text: None of the sources we can find today mark what year it was added.

mc5m.text: Some said it was a sea monster, a giant octopus.

mc5n.text: Later still, some counted her among the Bermuda Triangle cases.

mc5o.text: But she was found off the coast of Portugal.

mc5p.text: That's several thousand kilometers from Bermuda.

mc5q.text: The court files don't have a single word of any of this.

mc5r.text: The ship didn't even start out with that name.

mc5s.text: She was launched in Nova Scotia, Canada, in 1861, as the Amazon.

mc5t.text: Seven years later she was sold to Americans and only then renamed the Mary Celeste.

mc5u.text: A real ship's name, covered over by a story for more than a hundred years.

mc5v.text: So how did people at the time explain it themselves?

mc6a.text: Owner Winchester's account: the alcohol in the hold caught fire by itself.

mc6b.text: He said the fire blew the fore hatch cover open.

mc6c.text: But the hatch cover had been taken off and laid on the deck.

mc6d.text: And no one who boarded reported smelling anything.

mc6e.text: Nor was there any sign on board of burning or an explosion.

mc6f.text: Newspapers at the time also ran another version: she had been seized by pirates.

mc6g.text: But there wasn't a single sign of a struggle anywhere on board.

mc6h.text: Insurance fraud was something people guessed at even back then.

mc6i.text: Remember that share the captain had bought himself?

mc6j.text: If the ship sank, he was the one who would pay.

mc6k.text: Later researchers proposed an undersea earthquake, and a waterspout as well.

mc6l.text: But the ship the surveyor examined had even her cargo intact.

mc6m.text: So those two ideas are left as nothing more than hypotheses.

mc6n.text: That US warship captain also wrote one more line in his report.

mc6o.text: He said the reasons for abandoning this ship were not sufficient.

mc6p.text: In 2007, one study followed that same idea further.

mc6q.text: The chronometer was off; the captain was 120 miles west of where he thought.

mc6r.text: That sounding rod on the deck matters now.

mc6s.text: Of the two pumps, one had been taken apart.

mc6t.text: The previous voyage had carried coal, and coal dust may have clogged the pumps.

mc6u.text: Thinking the ship was about to sink is a call a captain would make.

mc6v.text: Both of these paths still have holes in them.

mc6w.text: But on the docks at Genoa, there's still one number nobody has mentioned.

mc7a.text: The ship reached Genoa, and the cargo was finally unloaded, barrel by barrel.

mc7b.text: Only then were those 1,701 barrels of alcohol actually counted.

mc7d.text: At Gibraltar the surveyor checked whether barrels were touched, not what was left.

mc7e.text: These nine were unlike the others: they were made of red oak.

mc7f.text: Red oak has large pores, so it leaks more easily.

mc7g.text: The most defensible version: the captain found water in the hold, or noticed a smell.

mc7h.text: He judged the ship was in danger and ordered everyone into the boat.

mc7i.text: Remember that thick broken rope at the stern?

mc7j.text: The boat was tied on at the end of the rope and towed along behind.

mc7l.text: The sails were still set, and the ship simply kept going.

mc7m.text: The boat was left on the sea, falling farther and farther behind.

mc7o.text: The same study used weather data to work that voyage backward.

mc7p.text: Its conclusion: the ship had essentially sailed on her own.

mc7q.text: Yet this explanation still can't account for the things missing from the list.

mc7r.text: People leaving a ship only for a while wouldn't take the navigation tools first.

mc7s.text: The boat and those ten people were never found.

mc7t.text: In 1885, a new captain ran her onto a reef to cheat the insurers.

mc7u.text: She didn't sink, the fraud was exposed, and the jury deadlocked seven to five.

mc7v.text: To this day, there is still no settled answer.

mc7w.text: They didn't vanish; they left, and couldn't get back.

mc7x.text: On why the ten left, what the record finally leaves is those nine empty barrels.

mc7y.text: Which version did you hear first?

mc7z.text: This channel tells only what's in the record. Subscribe to open the files with us.
